channel.title: California Uzbek — Latest
channel.description: Independent analysis · Central Asia & world geopolitics

item.title: Iran's IRGC says two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on November 5. The account has not been independently verified.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a Houthi missile fired toward Medina
item.description: The Saudi-led coalition said on November 5 that it had shot down a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis toward the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities.

item.title: How U.S. Bank Deposit Insurance (FDIC) Works
item.description: The FDIC is a federal system that protects a depositor's money with a government guarantee even if the bank fails. Coverage is automatic, up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category. Here is how it works.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed becomes the first Muslim US senator
item.description: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan in the November 3 midterms to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

item.title: US–Iran tensions open a door for China in the Persian Gulf
item.description: On November 3, Beijing held back-to-back meetings with Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia. The Guardian reports that America's confrontation with Iran is letting China expand its regional influence.

item.title: Uzbekistan extends its Work and Travel program to technical-college students
item.description: Under a Cabinet of Ministers resolution dated October 31, vocational (texnikum) students will be able to work abroad from the 2026/2027 academic year, with costs covered by a state loan.

item.title: The Turkestani Émigré Press: the Journals Yangi Turkistan and Yosh Turkistan (1927–1939)
item.description: Two journals published far from home in the Soviet era — Yangi Turkistan in Istanbul and Yosh Turkistan printed in Berlin — became the voice of Turkestan's émigré intellectuals. Here is their history, with exact dates and figures.

item.title: Child labor in Kyrgyzstan: poverty and gaps in enforcement
item.description: Dozens of children were found working at markets in the southern Kyrgyz city of Manas. A national survey found nearly one in five children aged 5–17 are in child labor.

item.title: How Tariffs and Customs Duties Work: Who Pays, and How Prices Are Affected
item.description: A tariff is a tax a government imposes on imported goods. It is paid at the border not by the foreign exporter but by the importer; studies find the cost is largely passed on to consumers through higher prices. Here is how the system works.

item.title: A ceasefire on paper: attacks continue in Gaza as Turkey urges the Islamic world to act
item.description: At the COMCEC meeting in Istanbul, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said massacres and aid obstruction persist despite the truce. Gaza authorities report 5,989 ceasefire violations.

item.title: Lured by 'work,' sent to war: how Russia recruits foreigners for the Ukraine front
item.description: Ukrainian intelligence says Russia is now also recruiting Indonesians through social media; Indonesia has formally objected. From Central Asia, hundreds have already been killed.

item.title: The Central Asian Union (1994): Economic Integration of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan
item.description: In the first years of independence, three Central Asian states — Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan — created a single economic space in 1994. It was the first major integration attempt led by the region itself, without Moscow.

item.title: “Second Chance”: 311 inmates in Uzbekistan are learning English and a trade
item.description: Across 11 penal institutions, 311 inmates aged 18–30 are being trained in English and computer literacy. In the first five months, 88.6% mastered the English A1 level and 79.5% reached computer-literacy proficiency.

item.title: California Proposition 40: a one-time 5% tax on billionaires goes to the voters
item.description: In the November 3 election, Californians voted on a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion. Backers project about $100bn over five years; some economists estimate about $30bn.

item.title: Your Rights in the U.S.: When Police or Immigration Agents Stop You
item.description: The U.S. Constitution gives every person — citizen or not — the right to remain silent, to refuse a search, and to ask for a lawyer. Here is how those rights work when police stop you on the street, in your car, or at your door.

item.title: US Supreme Court hears Catholic preschool case: a clash of religious freedom and LGBTQ rules
item.description: On November 3 the Court heard the Colorado Catholic preschools case. The schools call their exclusion from the state program religious discrimination; Colorado says the rules apply to everyone. A decision is expected by summer.

item.title: Labor Rights in the U.S.: Minimum Wage, Overtime, and Workplace Protections
item.description: In the U.S., federal law guarantees every worker — regardless of immigration status — a minimum wage, overtime pay above 40 hours, and a safe workplace. Here is how those rights work and where to turn if they are violated.

item.title: Uzbekistan finds six enterprises discharging untreated wastewater into open areas in Tashkent region
item.description: Six enterprises in the Yukorichirchiq district discharged production wastewater without adequate treatment. Lab tests showed suspended solids several times over the limit, and none of the firms held a positive environmental assessment.

item.title: The Soviet–Afghan War and Afghan Displacement (1979–1992): Afghan Uzbeks and the Refugee Wave
item.description: The 1979 Soviet invasion caused the largest refugee exodus since World War II — by 1989 more than six million Afghans had fled to Pakistan and Iran. The Afghan Uzbeks of the north were part of this displacement too.

item.title: The Creation of the Uzbek Presidency: Islam Karimov's Rise to Power (1989–1990)
item.description: On 23 June 1989 Islam Karimov became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Uzbekistan, and on 24 March 1990 he was elected President of the Uzbek SSR — the first such office created among the Soviet republics. Here is the history of those two dates.

item.title: Uzbekistan to open a migration center in every region: UZS 8bn each, with a push on German
item.description: Germany requested 45,000 specialists from Uzbekistan this year but hired only 2,000 — the main obstacle being a lack of German-language skills. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev ordered a single migration center in every region, each funded with UZS 8bn.

item.title: Uzbeks in trouble abroad to get help through the Online Mahalla platform
item.description: At a 2 November meeting the president put special focus on protecting the rights of citizens abroad: those in difficulty can leave a message on the Online Mahalla platform, and ambassadors will personally take up the case when needed; the system launches within 10 days.

item.title: US oil firms made $130bn in profit during the Iran war as household bills surged
item.description: According to Al Jazeera, US oil and gas firms earned more than $130bn in profit from April to September; Americans spent an extra $150bn on fuel, over $1,150 per household.

item.title: Mirziyoyev orders overhaul of labour migration: 'We need quality, not numbers'
item.description: At a 2 November meeting the president ordered better public awareness of overseas jobs, a migration centre in every region, and vocational and German-language training for young people; Germany requested 45,000 specialists but hired only 2,000.

item.title: Mirziyoyev: 'In migration, we need quality, not numbers' — overseas job placement to be handed to private agencies from 2027
item.description: On November 2, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev chaired a meeting on labour migration. Germany requested 45,000 specialists this year but only 2,000 Uzbeks were hired due to a German-language gap; from next year, overseas job placement will be transferred to private agencies.

item.title: The U.S. Visitor Visa (B-1/B-2): How Tourist and Business Travel Is Arranged
item.description: An Uzbekistan citizen travelling to the U.S. for tourism, to visit relatives, or for business needs a B-1/B-2 visa — because Uzbekistan is not in the visa-free program (Visa Waiver / ESTA). Here is a practical guide to the DS-160 form, the $185 fee, the interview, and how long you may stay.

item.title: Telegram leads news use in Uzbekistan, but television stays the most trusted
item.description: A national survey found 51.6% of people get news from Telegram, with TV second at 44.6%. On trust, however, television (44.3%) is far ahead of Telegram (11.3%).

item.title: Uzbekistan and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation: From the Shanghai Five to the SCO (1996–2001)
item.description: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) grew out of the 'Shanghai Five', formed in 1996 by China, Russia, and three Central Asian states. When Uzbekistan joined on 15 June 2001, the group became the SCO and Uzbekistan became one of its founding members. Here is that history — with precise dates and facts.

item.title: Cyberattack hits emergency-alert apps in Ukraine and Russia: fake nuclear warning in Kyiv
item.description: On Sunday both countries' emergency-alert mobile apps were hit by cyberattacks; users in Ukraine received a false warning of a nuclear radiation danger in Kyiv, while Russia said its ministry app had been breached.

item.title: As anti-Sharia politics intensify in Texas, Muslims prepare for the vote
item.description: Ahead of the US midterms, Texas Republicans are proposing to criminalize advocacy of Sharia and to denaturalize and deport its proponents. In response, the Muslim community is registering voters and fielding dozens of candidates.
